facts.fact_text: The present case concerns the applicant's prosecution in relation to his participation in peaceful assemblies.
On 4 December 2011 the applicant took part in a rally in St Petersburg.
The rally on 4 December 2011 in St Petersburg was a protest against the alleged fraud committed during the election to the State Duma on the same day.
On 6 December 2011 the applicant took part in another protest rally relating to the recent election to the State Duma.
On 26 November 2012 the applicant and several other people staged a 'performance' aimed at 'reviving' the Russian Constitution.
The 'performance' on 26 November 2012 consisted of a coffin filled with brochures containing the text of the Russian Constitution, and a speech.
During the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 the applicant held a poster saying 'Let us resurrect the Constitution'.
During the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 the applicant uttered several slogans including 'Follow your own laws', 'Stop the police state' and 'We need a different Russia'.
On 31 December 2012 the applicant took part in a rally at which the police were present.
On 5 April 2013 the applicant took part in a public assembly together with fewer than twenty people near the building of the St Petersburg Administration of the Bank of Russia.

It appears that the public assembly on 5 April 2013 was aimed at carrying the message that the Russian Government needed to prevent the removal of State-owned enterprises' revenues to offshore jurisdictions.
On 27 June 2013 the applicant and five others came in front of the building of the local office of the Federal Migration Service in St Petersburg.
On 27 June 2013 the applicant and another person climbed by a ladder onto the balcony at the first floor of the Federal Migration Service building in St Petersburg.
On the balcony of the Federal Migration Service building on 27 June 2013 the applicant and another person shouted the slogans 'FMS in Dushanbe' and 'Freedom to the people'.
On the balcony of the Federal Migration Service building on 27 June 2013 the applicant and another person unfolded a red flag with a white circle with a picture of a grenade.
The applicant was arrested following the rally on 4 December 2011 and taken to the police station.

On 7 February 2012 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 18 euros) for an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

On 7 February 2012 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 18 euros) for an offence under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The police arrested a number of people, including the applicant, at the rally on 6 December 2011.

On 7 December 2011 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to eleven days of detention for the offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences arising from the rally on 6 December 2011.
After the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 ended, the applicant was arrested and taken to the local police station.

On 17 December 2012 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to a fine of 15,000 Russian roubles (approximately 373 euros) under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences in relation to the 'performance' on 26 November 2012.
The applicant was arrested during the rally on 31 December 2012, allegedly prior to hearing any specific order from the police and, a fortiori, prior to disobeying any such order.

By a judgment issued on 1 January 2013 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg sentenced the applicant to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 17 euros) under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences in relation to the rally on 31 December 2012.

By a separate judgment issued on 1 January 2013 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg sentenced the applicant to a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately 497 euros) under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences in relation to the rally on 31 December 2012.
According to the applicant, when the public assembly on 5 April 2013 was about to end, the police arrived and arrested him and some other participants.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court sentenced the applicant on 21 November 2013 to a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately 450 euros at the time) in relation to the assembly on 5 April 2013.
Police officers arrived at the Federal Migration Service building and took the applicant to the local police station following the 'performance' on 27 June 2013.

On 8 October 2013 the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg convicted the applicant under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced him to a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately 456 euros) in relation to the 'performance' on 27 June 2013.

On 19 December 2013 the St Petersburg City Court reclassified the charge relating to the 'performance' on 27 June 2013 under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences and upheld the fine of 20,000 Russian roubles.

On 10 June 2013 the Nevskiy District Court of St Petersburg convicted the applicant under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences for organising and holding the public event on 5 April 2013 that had not been notified to the competent authority.
On 21 November 2013 the Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court reclassified the case relating to the assembly on 5 April 2013 under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
An offence report was compiled accusing the applicant of an offence under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences following the 'performance' on 27 June 2013.

The police considered that the 'performance' on 27 June 2013 amounted to an assembly regulated by the Public Events Act and thus required a prior notification to the St Petersburg city administration, but no such notification had been submitted.

The Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act) provides that the organiser of a public event must notify the executive or municipal authority of the event pursuant to sections 5 and 7 of the Act.

Section 6 § 3 of the Public Events Act provides that during a public event participants must comply with all lawful instructions given by the event organiser, the persons designated by the organiser, the designated representative of the executive authority of the constituency of the Russian Federation or the municipality, or by law enforcement officers.

Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided at the relevant time that disobedience to a lawful order or request made by a police officer, a military officer or a detention facility officer in connection with the exercise of duties relating to securing public order and public safety was punishable with a fine of 500 to 1,000 Russian roubles or administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided, prior to June 2012, that violation of the rules for running a public event was punishable by a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 Russian roubles as regards organisers.

Since June 2012 Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences was amended to contain a new paragraph 5 concerning participants, providing that violation by a participant in a public event of the rules for running a public event was punishable with a fine of from 10,000 to 20,000 Russian roubles or up to forty hours of community work.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg stated that in view of the political nature of the event on 6 December 2011 entailing expressions of discontent and the large number of demonstrators, there had been a 'real threat to other people'.

Pursuant to section 16 of the Public Events Act, the grounds for ending a public event shall be the emergence of a genuine threat to citizens' lives or health, and to the possessions of physical or legal persons.

Section 13 § 1 (1) and (7) of the Police Act (Federal Law no. 3-FZ of 7 February 2011) provides that outside the context of public events being held lawfully, the police is authorised to make an oral order requiring citizens to disperse or to go to another location where the amassing of people poses a threat to their lives or health, the lives or health of other citizens, possessions, or interferes with the work of organisations or impedes the traffic of vehicles or pedestrians.

The Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation held in Ruling no. 19-P of 17 May 2021 that legislative, regulatory or other measures on the part of public authorities should not unjustifiably restrict the constitutional right of peaceful assembly, and that restrictions should be based on the principles of necessity and proportionality, with due regard to the presumption in favour of the organisers' and demonstrators' willingness to maintain the peaceful nature of the event.
